exercises.title: Read a higher-order Church encoding
exercises.prompt: Let E=λm.λn.n m, with Church numerals m,n. Identify the arithmetic operation. Reduce E TWO THREE enough to count applications of f. Explain the n=0 case carefully: compare λx.x with the numeral ONE using β-reduction after supplying f and x. Also explain what λn.n(λx.FALSE)TRUE tests.
exercises.hint: Iterating the function TWO three times doubles the application count three times. Zero iterations returns the identity.
steps: E TWO THREE→THREE TWO→λx.TWO(TWO(TWO x)). Supplying f and then x shows 2³=8 applications of f, so the resulting numeral represents 8. Generally E m n represents m^n under Church arithmetic.
For n=0, ZERO m→λx.x. Applied to f and x this yields f x, the same as ONE f x. Thus it represents ONE extensionally, even though it is not the two-abstraction β-normal form λf.λx.f x.
At m=n=0 this encoding returns ONE as well: the encoding chooses the conventional Church-arithmetic value 0^0=1. It is not a claim about limits of real-valued exponentiation.
For the last term, zero applications of λx.FALSE leave TRUE; any positive numeral applies that constant-FALSE function at least once, yielding FALSE. It is a zero test.
exercises.scope: Direct written extensions of lambda-calculus lab exercises 2–3 and Church encodings.

exercises.title: A family ontology that reasons too far
exercises.prompt: Let isBrotherOf⊑isSiblingOf, with domain(isBrotherOf)=Male. Let isSiblingOf be symmetric and transitive, and Male⊓Female⊑⊥. ABox: isBrotherOf(a,b), Female(b). Is the KB consistent? Which sibling self-edges are entailed? Would making isBrotherOf symmetric preserve consistency? Explain the modelling issue without using Protégé.
exercises.hint: Properties of a superrole do not automatically become properties of its subrole. Symmetry plus transitivity creates self-edges.
steps: The KB is consistent. Infer Male(a) from the brother-role domain, isSiblingOf(a,b) by inclusion and isSiblingOf(b,a) by symmetry. No isBrotherOf(b,a) follows from those axioms.
Transitivity gives isSiblingOf(a,a) and isSiblingOf(b,b). A model can have distinct a,b, Male={a}, Female={b}, brother={(a,b)}, sibling={(a,a),(a,b),(b,a),(b,b)}.
If brother itself is symmetric, isBrotherOf(b,a) follows, so domain gives Male(b), clashing with Female(b) and disjointness.

A symmetric transitive role with any edge necessarily contains associated self-edges. If the intended sibling relation excludes self-siblings, that combination of axioms is unsuitable; the shared-parent rule in the lab uses explicit differentFrom instead of expecting these axioms to enforce distinctness.
exercises.scope: Family-ontology lab: role hierarchy, domain, symmetry, transitivity and disjointness.

exercises.title: When two existential witnesses must coincide
exercises.prompt: Relative to P⊓Q⊑⊥, is C=∃r.P⊓∃r.Q⊓(≤1 r.⊤) satisfiable? Give a semantic proof. Then examine the two repairs separately: remove the upper bound; or remove disjointness. For each repaired case give a smallest possible model and justify its size.
exercises.hint: Two existential statements may use one witness unless disjointness prevents it; the cardinality restriction then matters.
steps: If x∈C, choose an r-successor y∈P and z∈Q. The ≤1 bound forces y=z. That element is in P⊓Q, forbidden by the TBox; C is unsatisfiable.

Remove the upper bound: two domain elements suffice, not necessarily three. Take domain {x,y}, P={x}, Q={y}, r={(x,x),(x,y)}. Then x has both required successors, and P,Q are disjoint. One element cannot inhabit both nonempty disjoint fillers.
Remove disjointness instead: one element x suffices with P=Q={x} and r={(x,x)}. The one successor satisfies both existentials and the upper bound.

The source is allowed to be its own successor because no irreflexivity restriction was imposed. Requiring distinct names or forbidding self-edges without an axiom would incorrectly inflate the minimum.
rubric: Two-element first repair and lower bound
exercises.scope: DL restrictions, satisfiability, cardinalities and open-world model construction.
